submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole fires on concrete, particular everyday lifestyle-and-taste vocabulary - the word that names what people eat, drink, wear or do for leisure (food and drink: ' coffee', ' wine', ' pizza', ' burger', ' restaurant', ' cafe', ' deli'; clothing and personal goods: ' fashion', ' jewellery', ' boutique', ' shawl'; popular sports, pastimes and crafts: ' music', ' jazz', ' football', ' tennis', ' golf', ' snooker', ' rowing', ' pottery', ' violin', ' theatre', ' festival', ' dance') - which peaks at 0.5-4 (26-200% of the scan maximum, above the 0.25x active line) when such a word carries the clause's subject matter, while fine-art/abstract-culture vocabulary (' art', ' film', ' opera', ' painting', ' sculpture', ' literature', ' cinema', ' concert'), ordinary household objects and generic nouns (' table', ' window', ' mirror', ' office', ' geology', ' history') and function words stay at the floor. Two effects are not the content feature and should not be probed as one: a text's first token reads 0.5-0.8 for common function-word openers ('The', 'She', 'He', 'I', 'It'), so a probe opening with 'The' peaks near 0.65 whatever follows it, and the pole is retrospective - it nudges the token ' scene' in its output but shows no lookahead signal (correlation with next-token ' scene' probability -0.02).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee meeting began at seven in the community hall, with eleven residents seated in folding chairs along the back wall. The chairperson opened with a review of last month's minutes, which concerned parking permits, drainage on the eastern road, and the proposed replacement of two streetlights near the school crossing. A brief discussion followed about the budget shortfall, and the treasurer distributed a single-page summary showing that maintenance costs had risen by nine percent while the reserve fund had declined by roughly the same amount. Nobody objected to the figures, though one member asked whether the contractor's invoice for the drainage work had been received and whether it matched the original quote. The chairperson said it had arrived on Friday and would be circulated with the next mailing. The group then turned to the question of the autumn clean-up, which in previous years had involved volunteers working in pairs along the main road with gloves, bags, and a borrowed trailer. Several people noted that turnout had fallen and that a different approach might be needed, perhaps a single Saturday morning event advertised through the library and the notice boards. A subcommittee was formed, and its members agreed to meet separately before the next full session. The conversation moved to the allotment plots behind the church, where the soil had become compacted after the wet spring and where the water butt had developed a leak near its base. The treasurer offered to obtain three quotes for repairs and to report back. There was some confusion about whether the plot holders paid an annual fee to the parish or to the association, and the secretary promised to check the older records stored in the filing cabinet. At this point the chairperson introduced the item that had drawn most of the correspondence: a proposal from a nearby resident to run a series of evening classes in the hall during the winter months. The suggested subjects included basic accounting, conversational Spanish, and pottery, with the last of these described as suitable for complete beginners and requiring only a small kiln that could be housed in the storeroom. Members asked about insurance, heating costs, and the availability of the hall on weekday evenings. The secretary read aloud a letter from the resident explaining that an experienced instructor had already agreed to teach the sessions and that materials could be supplied at cost. After some debate the committee voted to approve the proposal in principle, subject to a written risk assessment and a confirmed booking schedule. The meeting closed at ten past nine, and the remaining items were deferred to the following month. The secretary agreed to circulate the revised draft by email, and the chairperson reminded everyone that the hall would be unavailable during the first week of December because the floor was being resealed. Two members offered to help move the tables and chairs into the storeroom on the Saturday before, and the treasurer said he would bring a trolley.
